text.p: These are the leading stories in the Namibian press on Friday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Accused child rapist Nangombe Kalukambe faced the wrath of hundreds of women and men when he appeared in court at Tsumeb on Thursday charged with the brutal rape of a two-year-old toddler. Angry demonstrators rushed to grab him as he was bundled out of the court after the hearing. He was remanded in custody until July 24. In Windhoek, over 500 people demonstrated in front of the High Court calling for stricter action on violence against women and children.

- European non-governmental organisations involved in facilitating the tour of two Himba headmen have fired back against criticism from the Namibian government. The groups dismissed claims that the chiefs were being used as their tools to undermine the Namibian economy. In an open letter to the Ministry of Mines and Energy, the groups also stated that they were not only environmental groups, but also included United Nations accredited human rights groups.

- First National Bank Namibia has anounced that the fifth biggest bank in the world, Fuji Bank in London, and a consortium of investors have approved a loan of $30 million. The loan, which is to be paid back in a year's time, was offered to First National Bank at LIBOR rates plus five percent. The move was seen as a sign of trust in Namibia, as it is only the second country in Africa to be able to lend money on the international market.

- The Epupa dam project and Himba opposition to it have once again resulted in racist remarks and allegations of European connivance against the Namibian government. The remarks were aired on the call-in programme of the Oshiwambo Service of the national broadcaster NBC. The programme, in which deputy minister of mines and energy Jesaja Nyamu made an appearance, was characterised by degrading statements about the Himba people, and allegations that a German, an American and a DTA leader are behind eery Himba headman opposed to the construction of the Epupa hydro-electric scheme.

- Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe were on Thursday overjoyed at being given the green light for limited trade in ivory at the CITES meeting in Harare. But those opposing the vote criticised the fact that there was no time for debate over the re-worked proposals and the voting system of CITES in which abstentions are not taken into consideration. Fourteen EU countries had abstained from the vote.

- Police in Tsumeb have arrested and detained an elderly jealous husband for slicing off part of his wife's vagina, stabbing her several times with a knife and fracturing her jaw. The incident took place on Wednesday, just a day before the court appearance of another Tsumeb resident, who had raped a toddler.
- Four police detective officers in Oshakati face charges of assault using excessive force and torture to extract information from a suspect currently in police detention.
